Project 01  /  SolidWorks & ANSYS

Rotors

Taking mass out of the spinning parts.

Scope
Four rotors, front and rear
Material
4140 steel, 3.175 mm
Tools
SolidWorks, ANSYS
Status
Design of record
Goal

Cut weight from the rotors. They are unsprung and spinning, so every gram costs the car twice — once as mass, again as inertia.

Challenges
  • The hub interface was fixed, so weight could only come out of the ring that sheds heat. Mass and thermal margin were in direct conflict.
  • ANSYS reported a peak stress at the pad contact edge that climbed every time I refined the mesh — 1,323 to 1,834 to 3,787 MPa. A real stress settles under refinement. This one never did, so it is an artifact of the model.

Rotor mass, before and after

SolidWorks mass properties, measured on each part — not estimated from the drawing.

BeforeAfter
Front rotor
474 g
415 g
Rear rotor
342 g
284 g

Bars to a common 500 g scale. Whole car: 1,633 g → 1,396 g.

Result
  • 236 g of rotating mass off the car, with polar inertia down 22 % at both ends — about six times what a different steel would have saved.
  • Safety factor 2.9 against a target of 1.5, taken from the converged result below the surface, where three meshes agree within 3 %.
  • 6.7 % thermal margin at the worst case. The lighter rotor runs hotter, reaching 502 °C against the pad's 538 °C ceiling. That is the thinnest number in the system, so it goes on the review slide.
Project 02  /  SolidWorks & race telemetry

Pedal box

Everything the driver does enters the system here.

Scope
Pedal, cylinders, balance bar
Pedal
6061-T6, 4.85:1 ratio
Design load
2,000 N at the pad
Status
Design of record
Goal

Make sure the pedal survives a panic stop, and that the braking it produces is split correctly between the front and rear wheels.

Challenges
  • The first analysis put peak stress at the pivot boss with a safety factor of 1.6 — passing, but thin for the one part whose failure leaves the driver with no brakes.
  • I had specified a smaller rear master cylinder to hit a brake bias rule of thumb from the reference books. I had applied it without checking it against this car.

Measured pedal force against the load I designed to

Back-calculated from logged line pressure at the team's 4.85:1 pedal ratio, across two competitions.

Endurance, hardest stop
580 N
Autocross, hardest stop
740 N
Brake test, all four wheels locked
1,430 N
The load I designed to
2,000 N

Bars to a common 2,000 N scale. The design load sits above anything a driver has produced.

Result
  • Safety factor 1.6 to 2.0 by enlarging one fillet, at almost no added weight. That pedal is the design of record.
  • I reversed my own decision and kept the original cylinder. 17 logs of race data showed the car already runs close to ideal bias for its own weight distribution. The smaller bore would have pushed ideal bias outside the balance bar's range at higher deceleration. The rule of thumb was right in general and wrong for this car.
  • Design deceleration set at 1.30 g from a measured brake test with all four wheels locked, replacing an assumed figure.
Project 03  /  Test hardware · in build

Brake dynamometer

Building the instrument the subteam did not have.

Scope
Concept to firmware, solo
Drive
PM DC treadmill motor
Logging
Teensy, four channels
Status
Electronics in build
Goal

Measure pad friction directly. It sets brake torque, and brake torque sets everything else — bias, pedal force, rotor temperature. For this team it had only ever been a catalog number.

Challenges
  • No budget for a commercial dyno, so the rig comes out of a repurposed treadmill motor and parts already in the shop.
  • Torque is expensive to measure on a spinning shaft. Instead the caliper floats on a reaction arm that bears on a load cell, turning torque into a force on a known lever.
  • A bench rig can quietly mislead you, so I wrote its limits down first: it measures friction and fade, while bias, lock-up order and stopping distance stay on the car.
Where it stands
  • Designed solo, instrumentation under $400. Four channels log speed, torque, line pressure and rotor temperature.
  • Mechanical design is set and the drive electronics are being wired. No friction data has been taken yet.
  • It anchors a validation plan I wrote covering 21 planned tests across simulation, bench, on-car and inspection, each with its own pass criteria.
Outside school

Heavy equipment, hands on

My family's business — operating the machines and doing the mechanic work on them.

The work

I grew up running and repairing heavy equipment in my family's business — hydraulics, drivetrain and structural repair, on machines that had to work the next morning. That is a different kind of deadline than a lab report.

What it gave me
  • It is why I was useful in the Formula SAE shop in my first week rather than my second year. I already knew how to run the machines and make something instead of waiting for someone else to make it.
  • It is where the dynamometer came from. Building a test rig out of a treadmill motor and a load cell is the same instinct as fixing a machine with what is on the shelf.
What I bring

Design that has to survive being checked

Looking for a summer 2027 engineering internship in aerospace, defense or ground robotics.

The through line is not that I picked good designs. It is that I built the evidence that says whether a design is good, and followed it when it disagreed with me. I have withdrawn a failure prediction I had already presented, reversed a hardware decision I had specified, and refused to report a stress number the software handed me. I would rather give a reviewer the thinnest margin in the system than have them find it.
